Most people present a chart the same way. They put it on the screen and they describe it from left to right. In January the number was this, in February it was that. By March, the room has stopped listening. Here is what I teach instead. Before you show the chart, say one sentence that tells the whole story. Something like: our costs have climbed steadily for three years, and this quarter they rose sharply. Now the audience knows what to look for. Then give them only three numbers: where it started, where it ended, and how big the change was. From four million to six million, an increase of fifty percent. That is enough. Nobody remembers the fifth number. And finish with why it matters. A chart without a so what is just decoration.

And now a look at coffee. Prices for arabica beans have had a remarkable year. In January they were trading at about two dollars a pound. By the end of March, after a long dry season in Brazil, they had climbed to almost three dollars. Then, in May, they plunged by twenty percent in a single week, when the rain finally came. Since June, prices have fluctuated between two dollars forty and two dollars seventy. Analysts expect them to edge up again before the end of the year, as demand from Asia continues to grow steadily. For coffee drinkers, the news is mixed. Your morning cup probably won't get cheaper, but the sharp spike of last spring is unlikely to return. That's the market report for this week.
